title: Getting climate into culture
gist: Despite years of industry pledges and Hollywood climate summits, measurement tools like the 'Bechdel test for climate' show climate change barely appears in film and TV, and theatre's rare successes — including the new musical Hot Mess, which reframes the climate crisis as a breakup between Earth and Humanity — have worked by avoiding didacticism rather than embracing it.

insights.claim: Despite mounting evidence of climate change's severe consequences, the scale of climate protest seen in 2019 — the biggest in history — has not been repeated since.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Suggests public mobilisation on climate has stalled even as the underlying crisis has worsened, framing the cultural-representation problem the article investigates.
insights.quote: despite the mounting evidence of the severe consequences of climate change, 2019’s large-scale protests have not been repeated
insights.locator: Almost seven years later, Hot Mess opened

insights.claim: Although European and US publics understand climate change as a serious crisis, it barely shows up as a theme in popular culture, despite considerable effort by artists, philanthropists and industry summits.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: States the article's core puzzle: public concern about climate has not translated into cultural representation.
insights.quote: while European and US publics understand climate change as a serious crisis, it barely shows up as a theme in popular culture.
insights.locator: In his prison notebooks, Antonio Gramsci

insights.claim: Antonio Gramsci wrote in his prison notebooks about the essential role of culture in generating political change, a framework the article uses to explain why climate's cultural absence matters for political mobilisation.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Provides the theoretical rationale for why entertainment industry failure to depict climate change has political consequences.
insights.quote: In his prison notebooks, Antonio Gramsci wrote about the essential role of culture in generating political change

themes.theme: Measuring climate's absence: film and TV data

insights.claim: Good Energy, a US non-profit founded by Anna Jane Joyner, and Rice University's Dr Matthew Schneider-Mayerson developed the Climate Reality Check, popularly known as the 'Bechdel test for climate', which a story passes only if it's clear climate change is happening in the story's world and at least one character shows awareness of it.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Gives investors and media analysts a concrete, named methodology for measuring climate representation in entertainment output.
insights.quote: A storyline set on Earth in the present or the near future passes the test only if it’s clear in the world of the story that climate change is happening, and if at least one character demonstrates that they know it’s happening.
insights.locator: The US-based non-profit consultancy Good Energy

insights.claim: Fewer than 10 per cent of the 250 most popular films released between 2013 and 2022 passed the Climate Reality Check.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how rarely climate change appears even implicitly in mainstream, high-audience films over a decade.
insights.quote: It was a test that fewer than 10 per cent of the 250 most popular films released in the decade between 2013 and 2022 passed.
insights.locator: It was a test that fewer than 10 per cent

insights.claim: Of 2024's Oscar-nominated feature films, only three of 13 eligible films passed the Climate Reality Check, including — implausibly — Barbie.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Shows even prestige, critically lauded cinema mostly fails to acknowledge climate change, with the rare pass being an unexpected outlier.
insights.quote: For 2024’s Oscar-nominated movies, only three out of 13 eligible feature-length films did so—implausibly, one of them Barbie.

insights.claim: A separate Good Energy report found that just 2.8 per cent of 37,453 scripted television episodes and films released between 2016 and 2020 included any mention of climate change, and even when extreme weather appeared as a plot backdrop it was rarely connected to fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Extends the representation gap from prestige film to the much larger volume of scripted TV, showing the problem is systemic across formats.
insights.quote: just 2.8 per cent of 37,453 scripted television episodes and films released between 2016 and 2020 included any mention of climate change, even as a backdrop to other plots, and where extreme weather events featured in the plotlines, they were rarely connected to fossil fuels
insights.locator: Another report that Good Energy commissioned

insights.claim: Twelve UK and Irish broadcasters and streamers, including the BBC, Channel 4, ITV and Warner Bros Discovery, signed BAFTA Albert's Climate Content Pledge at Cop26 in Glasgow in November 2021, and by May 2026 the pledge had expanded to include Banijay UK, Fremantle and ITV Studios, representing over 100 production companies globally — yet the pledges' impact on actual content remains marginal.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Shows industry-level commitments have scaled significantly without producing measurable change in on-screen climate representation.
insights.quote: But despite the pledges, the impact remains marginal.
insights.locator: But despite the pledges, the impact remains marginal

insights.claim: Roland Emmerich's The Day After Tomorrow (2004) pioneered squeezing climate change into the disaster-movie format, connecting natural disasters directly to climate change and stimulating vigorous if partisan debate, despite being scientifically inaccurate.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Identifies the earliest major Hollywood attempt at climate storytelling and its trade-off between accuracy and public engagement.
insights.quote: Hollywood began by squeezing climate change into the disaster movie format, notably in Roland Emmerich’s The Day After Tomorrow (2004).
insights.locator: Hollywood began by squeezing climate change

insights.claim: Where climate change is directly and earnestly addressed, as in Apple TV+'s 2023 series Extrapolations, critics have judged the results dull despite good intentions.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Illustrates a recurring pattern: direct, message-driven climate content tends to underperform critically even when well-funded.
insights.quote: Where climate change is directly addressed, as in Apple TV+’s 2023 series Extrapolations, critics have judged the results earnest but dull.
insights.locator: Where climate change is directly addressed

insights.claim: Greenland, a collectively written climate play by Moira Buffini, Penelope Skinner, Matt Charman and Jack Thorne that premiered at the National Theatre, was described by Thorne as one of the worst-reviewed plays the National Theatre has ever staged.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: A concrete, high-profile failure case illustrating the risk of didactic, ensemble-written climate theatre.
insights.quote: Thorne recently described it as one of the worst-reviewed plays the National Theatre has ever staged.
insights.locator: Greenland, a climate play collectively written

insights.claim: Kyoto, a play about the Kyoto Protocol negotiations by Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson, succeeded where other climate theatre failed, likely because its main character was not a heroic scientist but an outright villain sabotaging the negotiations on behalf of fossil fuel interests.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Suggests a specific dramaturgical lesson: climate stories work better with a compelling antagonist than a righteous protagonist.
insights.quote: created a gripping and highly successful drama about the unlikely subject of the Kyoto Protocol negotiations—perhaps because their main character was not a heroic scientist but an outright villain, intent on sabotage on behalf of fossil fuel interests
insights.locator: In contrast to Greenland’s didactic approach

insights.claim: The Contingency Plan by Steve Waters, two full-length plays set in the near-future UK and centred on a scientist battling an indifferent bureaucratic and political class, was well received at the Bush Theatre in 2009 and shortlisted for the John Whiting Award.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: An early counterexample of successful climate theatre, providing a contrast point for later, less successful efforts.
insights.quote: One early and well-received effort, The Contingency Plan, by the British playwright Steve Waters, ... It opened at the Bush Theatre in April 2009 and was shortlisted for the John Whiting Award.
insights.locator: In theatre, too, success has been elusive

themes.theme: Hot Mess: origin and creative choices

insights.claim: Hot Mess creators Jack Godfrey and Ellie Coote began writing the musical in September 2019, when the largest climate protests in history had just happened, and it finally opened at the Other Palace theatre roughly seven years later during a heatwave coinciding with London Climate Action Week.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Shows the show's long, multi-year development arc from concept to critically acclaimed staging.
insights.quote: In September 2019, when Jack Godfrey and Ellie Coote began to work on what became Hot Mess (currently playing at the Other Palace theatre in London), the moment felt urgent

insights.claim: Hot Mess originated when Jack Godfrey, cycling to work while singing a breakup song called 'Used to Be', realised the song could be reimagined as sung by humanity to the Earth, spawning the show's central metaphor of a romantic relationship between Earth and Humanity.
insights.speaker: Jack Godfrey
insights.so_what: A specific, memorable origin story for the show's core creative conceit.
insights.quote: I was cycling to work one day, singing this song in my head, tears rolling down my cheeks, when I thought, what if this song was being sung by humanity to the Earth?
insights.locator: At the time, Godfrey was going through

insights.claim: Godfrey and Coote pitched the Earth-Humanity relationship idea at Beam, a biennial musical theatre event, where producer Vicky Graham commissioned them to write it; the show then went through a 2021 Dundee concert performance, a 2025 Edinburgh Fringe run and a Southwark Playhouse London debut before reaching the Other Palace.
insights.speaker: Isabel Hilton
insights.so_what: Traces the commercial and production pathway that took the show from pitch to full London staging.
insights.quote: They pitched the idea at Beam, a biennial event for musical theatre, and producer Vicky Graham commissioned them to write it.
insights.locator: They pitched the idea at Beam

insights.claim: Godfrey and Coote found that once they committed to Earth and Humanity as a real relationship, the material demanded becoming more of an out-and-out comedy, letting audiences lean into the premise's absurdity rather than treating it earnestly.
insights.speaker: Ellie Coote
insights.so_what: A specific craft lesson on why comedy, not didacticism, made the show work — reinforcing the article's broader pattern.
insights.quote: Once we accepted that this was going to be a real relationship between Earth and Humanity, it forced us to make it more of an out-and-out comedy. When you start the show in that absurd way, you have to go for it, to allow people to lean in and acknowledge the absurdity of it.
insights.locator: Godfrey and Coote admit there were many lessons

insights.claim: Godfrey and Coote deliberately chose not to resolve the climate crisis in Hot Mess's ending, deciding instead to 'take the pressure off' since they don't have the answers, aiming to give audiences space to feel rather than instructions to follow.
insights.speaker: Ellie Coote
insights.so_what: Articulates a deliberate creative philosophy for climate art: process over prescription, feeling over homework.
insights.quote: We are not giving people homework, but it’s immeasurable how art impacts people. We want to give audiences the space and time to think and feel about the climate crisis, to sit in their feelings, however absurd and uncomfortable that might be, and to experience that together.
